title: Dhammas: the four truths
hookLine: he knows as it really is: this is dukkha, its arising, its ceasing, the way (MN 10)

lines: CAN IT GET BETTER? WHAT'S THE TREATMENT?
THE SHAPE OF THE FIRST TEACHING.
cards: A good doctor does four things, usually in this order. What's wrong? What's causing it?
Can it get better? What's the treatment? Skip a step and things go badly.
Treat the symptom without the cause, and it comes back. Believe it can't get better, and you won't try. Teachers often point out that the Buddha's first teaching has this same shape.
And the Satipatthana Sutta, after everything else, ends its tour of the four foundations right back at that first teaching. Today: dhammas, the four truths.

teach.h: THE FOUR TRUTHS, WATCHED, NOT ONLY BELIEVED.
teach.b: You met the four noble truths long ago on this path. Here, the sutta turns them into something to watch, not only a teaching to hold.
The practitioner knows, as it really is: this is dukkha, the unsatisfactoriness, the stress and pain of life. This is the arising of dukkha. This is the ceasing of dukkha.
This is the way leading to its ceasing.
As it really is, in Pali yathabhutam, is the key phrase: seeing things the way they are, not the way you're afraid they are or wish they were.
Notice where the truths come: at the very end of the fourth foundation, after the body, feelings, mind, the hindrances, the heaps, the sense bases, and the factors of awakening.
As if all that watching was training the eyes to see the biggest pattern of all, right inside ordinary experience.

teach.h: A TIGHT CHEST IN FOUR STEPS.
teach.b: A tight chest before a meeting: this is dukkha. Wanting it to go perfectly: that's its arising. The moment you let go of needing it perfect, and the chest loosens: that's its ceasing, even if only for a moment.
And the whole practice you've been learning, the breath, the knowing, the kindness: that's the way. The longer version of the sutta, in the Long Discourses, spells each truth out at length.
The shorter one keeps it to four plain lines.
Either way, the instruction is the same: know it, as it is.

how: Buddhist teachers often present the four noble truths in the pattern of a physician's diagnosis, and in insight meditation they are contemplated directly in experience rather than only studied as doctrine.

o: sacred laws handed down from heaven to obey
patterns to see: dukkha, its cause, its end, the way
beliefs a Buddhist must accept before practicing

games.q: match each truth to the doctor's question.

s: the four truths come at the very end of the fourth foundation
after the hindrances, heaps, sense bases and factors of awakening.
'as it really is' means seeing things as we hope they are
yathabhutam means seeing them the way they are, not as we fear or wish.
the longer version of the sutta spells the truths out at length
the Maha-satipatthana Sutta in the Long Discourses.

games.q: your chest tightens before a meeting. the sutta asks you to know the four truths in this. what is 'the arising'?
o: the wanting for it to go perfectly.
games.why: in the four truths, dukkha arises from craving. the wanting feeds the tightness; its easing is the ceasing.

practice: Bring to mind one small problem, not the biggest one, and walk it through four steps: what the discomfort is, plainly; what wanting, or not-wanting, is feeding it; what it would feel like, even for a breath, for that wanting to relax; and what one small, wise step you could take.
Then let the problem go, and rest with the breath.

wordCard.voice: Dhammas, the four truths. Dukkha, its arising, its ceasing, and the way: known, as it really is, inside ordinary experience.

orig.note: Pali yathābhūta: as it really is, the way the truths are to be known.

carryVoice: Your line: know it as it is. The biggest pattern, seen in the smallest moments. Day two hundred sixty-four, done.

sources.ref: Majjhima Nikāya 10 (Satipaṭṭhāna Sutta), the four noble truths
